summaries.example: Imagine drawing a line without lifting your pencil. The line looks unbroken, even though you can keep zooming in and dividing it into smaller pieces. A pebble collection is different: its pieces are separate. Some mathematicians have wondered whether a smooth line is really made from tiny pieces, or whether it is more basic than any collection of separate points.
summaries.summary: This entry studies a big question about mathematics and philosophy: what is a continuum? A continuum is something that seems unbroken, such as a line, space, time, or motion. Its opposite is the discrete, made of separate pieces. The entry also follows the history of infinitesimals—quantities treated as extremely small, sometimes smaller than every ordinary amount but not zero. Ancient thinkers argued about whether continuous things could be divided forever or were made from atoms. Later mathematicians used indivisibles and infinitesimals to develop calculus. Because their meaning seemed puzzling, nineteenth-century mathematicians built calculus around limits and numbers instead. In the twentieth century, new systems made rigorous use of infinitesimals again. Nonstandard analysis uses special numbers that can be infinitely large or infinitesimally small. Smooth infinitesimal analysis uses nonzero quantities whose square can be zero. Constructive and intuitionistic approaches offer different ideas about how real numbers and the continuum can be formed and known.
key_ideas: A continuum is understood as something connected or unbroken, while a discrete collection has separate parts.
People have disagreed about whether a continuous line can be built from tiny points or atoms.
Infinitesimals were useful in developing calculus, but many mathematicians worried that they were not logically clear.
Later theories gave infinitesimals careful mathematical homes, including nonstandard analysis and smooth infinitesimal analysis.
Other approaches, including constructive and intuitionistic mathematics, ask what it means for a mathematical object to be built or known.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question of continuity appears in drawings, motion, time, space, and calculus. It also shows that mathematics is not only about calculating answers. Mathematicians sometimes debate what kinds of things numbers, points, lines, and tiny quantities really are. Studying these debates helps us see why clear definitions matter and why more than one mathematical framework can illuminate the same idea.

important_terms.definition: Something that is unbroken and has no gaps, such as an ideal line or a stretch of time.
Being made of separate pieces, like scattered pebbles.
A quantity that is not zero but is smaller than every ordinary positive amount in a chosen mathematical system.
A part that cannot be divided into smaller parts.
A mathematical idea for finding change and areas; it uses limits, or in some approaches infinitesimals.

questions_to_think_about: Can a line be made from points, or is a line something different from a pile of points?
If you keep cutting a piece of string in half, do you ever reach a final, uncut piece?
Why might a useful math idea still need a careful explanation?
Would a moving object make more sense as a smooth process or as many tiny jumps?

summaries.example: Consider the function f(x)=x² near x=3. In a limit-based treatment, continuity says that when x is made sufficiently close to 3, f(x) becomes as close as desired to f(3)=9. In nonstandard analysis, one can instead use a nonzero infinitesimal h: continuity is expressed by f(3+h) being infinitesimally close to f(3). In smooth infinitesimal analysis, a special h with h²=0 gives f(3+h)=f(3)+f′(3)h, displaying the tangent behavior directly. These are different rigorous settings, not simply different names for the same object.
summaries.summary: “Continuity and Infinitesimals” traces changing answers to two connected questions: what makes a domain continuous, and how can mathematics describe quantities smaller than every ordinary positive quantity? A continuum is characterized informally by connectedness and absence of gaps; the discrete consists of separated units. Ancient debates opposed atomist accounts, which reduced extension to atoms, to views associated with Aristotle, for whom a continuum is not a collection of indivisibles and is divisible without a final division. Early modern calculus made infinitesimals productive tools for slopes, areas, and changing quantities, but critics questioned whether such entities were neither zero nor ordinary nonzero quantities. Limits, together with the arithmetization of the real line by figures such as Weierstrass, Dedekind, and Cantor, supplied a more rigorous classical foundation. Yet this did not settle the philosophical issue. Brentano, Peirce, Brouwer, and Weyl challenged, in different ways, the idea that an intuitive continuum is exhausted by a set of completed points. Twentieth-century developments reopened the subject. Nonstandard analysis extends the real numbers with hyperreals and uses transfer to connect infinitesimal reasoning with ordinary analysis. Smooth infinitesimal analysis instead works with nilpotent infinitesimals and an intuitionistic logic in which classical excluded middle does not generally hold. Constructive and intuitionistic approaches further distinguish completed mathematical objects from objects obtained through explicit or ongoing construction.
key_ideas: The historical opposition between continuity and discreteness includes both metaphysical questions about reality and technical questions about mathematical foundations.
Aristotle defended the irreducibility of the continuum to indivisibles, while atomist traditions treated matter or extension as ultimately discrete; later thinkers developed varied positions.
Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century calculus relied heavily on indivisibles, differentials, and infinitesimals, even while their logical status was disputed.

Nineteenth-century analysis increasingly replaced fixed infinitesimals with limits and arithmetical constructions of the real numbers. Weierstrass, Dedekind, and Cantor each contributed to this shift.
Critics of arithmetization, including Brouwer and Weyl, argued in different ways that an intuitive continuum should not simply be identified with a completed collection of discrete points.
Modern alternatives revive infinitesimals in distinct ways: nonstandard analysis uses hyperreal numbers, while smooth infinitesimal analysis uses nilpotent infinitesimals and intuitionistic logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history shows that “continuity” is not a single unquestioned idea. It can mean connectedness, infinite divisibility, smooth change, a topological property, or a feature of an intended mathematical model. Likewise, “infinitesimal” can refer to a vanishing sequence, a hyperreal smaller than every reciprocal of a natural number, or a nilpotent quantity. These distinctions matter because the foundations of calculus influence what counts as a proof, an object, and an acceptable explanation of change.

important_terms.definition: An unbroken whole, traditionally associated with lines, space, time, motion, or continuous variation.
The view that a continuum can be divided again and again without ending in indivisible parts.
A quantity treated as nonzero yet smaller than every finite positive quantity, although its exact meaning depends on the mathematical theory.
A part with no proper parts; an indivisible is not automatically infinitesimal or extended.
A precise account of approaching a value, used in nineteenth-century foundations of calculus.
The program of grounding analysis in arithmetical structures rather than geometric or motion-based intuition.
Robinson’s theory, using mathematical logic, in which hyperreal numbers include infinitely large and infinitesimal numbers and preserve ordinary first-order properties through transfer.
A category-theoretic framework in which nilpotent infinitesimals support a smooth, limit-free treatment of differentiation and continuity.

questions_to_think_about: Does defining the real line as a number system explain continuity, or does it merely model some properties of a continuum?
What is gained, and what may be lost, when geometric or temporal intuition is replaced by arithmetical definitions?
Why can a theory allow an infinitesimal quantity while rejecting the classical law that every quantity is either zero or nonzero?
How do nonstandard analysis and smooth infinitesimal analysis differ in what counts as an infinitesimal?
Should a mathematical theory require an object to be explicitly constructible before saying that it exists?

summaries.example: Think about zooming in on a curved road. From far away it bends, but a very small piece can look almost straight. One way to describe this uses a limit: as the piece becomes shorter and shorter, its direction approaches the road’s tangent direction. Another mathematical system uses an infinitesimal piece that is not ordinary zero. In that system, the road can be treated as straight on that tiny scale. The two descriptions can agree about results while using different ideas about what the tiny piece is.
summaries.summary: The entry explores how philosophers and mathematicians have understood continuity, discreteness, and infinitesimals. A continuum is an unbroken whole, while a discrete thing has separate members. Lines, space, time, and motion are common examples of continua, but thinkers have disagreed about whether a continuum can be reduced to points or atoms. Aristotle argued that a continuous magnitude is divisible without reaching a final indivisible part; atomists argued that matter or extension is ultimately made from discrete atoms. In the early modern period, indivisibles and infinitesimals became important tools for calculating areas, volumes, slopes, and motion. Their usefulness did not remove doubts about their meaning. During the nineteenth century, limits and arithmetical constructions of the real numbers became central to rigorous analysis. This “arithmetization” treated the continuum through numbers and sets, but some philosophers and mathematicians continued to argue that an intuitive continuum has features not captured by separate points. Later work developed several alternatives. Nonstandard analysis introduced hyperreal numbers, including genuine infinitesimal numbers within an extended system. Smooth infinitesimal analysis used nilpotent infinitesimals and treated the continuous as fundamental rather than explainable entirely through the discrete. Constructive and intuitionistic mathematics also reconsidered what it means for real numbers and continuous objects to exist.
key_ideas: Continuity suggests connection and unity; discreteness suggests separation and plurality.
A central disagreement is whether a line is composed of points or whether points and other small parts only describe aspects of a line.
Ancient Greek philosophers connected the issue to motion, change, and the relation between the One and the Many.
Infinitesimals helped mathematicians develop calculus, but their unclear status led nineteenth-century mathematicians to emphasize limits and rigorous definitions of real numbers.
Weierstrass, Dedekind, and Cantor developed arithmetical ways to describe the real line, while Brouwer and Weyl questioned whether this captured the intuitive continuum completely.
Modern theories do not simply return to old informal infinitesimals: nonstandard analysis and smooth infinitesimal analysis give them different rigorous roles.
summaries.why_it_matters: Calculus describes changing quantities, curves, motion, and areas, so its foundations depend on what “continuous” and “infinitely small” mean. The entry also shows how mathematical ideas change: an approach may be rejected as unclear, then later return in a new, rigorous form. Comparing these approaches helps us separate a calculation’s usefulness from the deeper assumptions that explain why the calculation works.

important_terms.definition: A whole with no gaps, such as an ideal line, while still allowing division into smaller parts.
A collection whose members are separate rather than joined into one unbroken whole.
A supposed quantity smaller than every finite positive quantity but not equal to zero; different theories define this differently.
A part that cannot itself be divided; a point is one possible example in geometry.
The value that a quantity approaches as it gets closer and closer to a target.
A mathematical framework that uses hyperreal numbers, including infinitely large and infinitesimal numbers.
An approach that treats mathematical existence as requiring an explicit construction, at least in principle.

questions_to_think_about: If a line has infinitely many points, does that mean it is made out of points?
Why might mathematicians replace a helpful but vague idea with a less intuitive definition?
Can two mathematical theories describe the same curve or motion while disagreeing about what the tiny pieces are?
What difference does it make whether a number is already completed or can only be approximated?
Why might someone think that a continuous whole cannot be split into two separate pieces?
